notes: Burchell unfair dismissal substitution error; appeal remitted de novo.

enrichment.short_title: Burchell test and tribunal substitution in unfair dismissal
key_facts: Mr Burkett, a Post Office driver with nearly ten years' unblemished service, was summarily dismissed after seriously overfilling a vehicle with oil, causing about £6,000 damage.
The employer believed he had deliberately overfilled the vehicle to avoid using it; the Employment Tribunal found unfair dismissal with 30% contributory fault and awarded £3,111.50.

The EAT dismissed the employer's appeal, but the Court of Appeal held the tribunal had substituted its own factual view for the employer's rather than asking whether the employer had reasonable grounds for its belief.
The court allowed the appeal and remitted the case to a different Employment Tribunal for a hearing de novo.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal after an unfair dismissal finding in favour of the employee.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the case was remitted to a different Employment Tribunal for a fresh hearing.
enrichment.ratio: On an unfair dismissal claim, an employment tribunal must apply the Burchell test by asking whether the employer had reasonable grounds for its honest belief in misconduct based on the facts before the employer after a reasonable investigation; it must not substitute its own assessment of whether the conduct was deliberate.
legal_issues: Proper application of British Home Stores v Burchell
Whether the tribunal substituted its own view of deliberateness
Distinction between adequacy of investigation and reasonable grounds for belief
Whether the Court of Appeal should remit or finally determine fairness

confidence.notes: Outcome, Burchell reasoning, and remission order are explicit in the approved judgment.

notes: Reinstatement of struck-out asylum JR refused for lack of merits, delay, and untruthfulness.

enrichment.short_title: Reinstatement of struck-out asylum judicial review
key_facts: Mr Idubo, an unsuccessful asylum applicant, sought to reinstate a judicial review application that had been struck out when he failed to appear before Buxton LJ.
The underlying challenge was to a special adjudicator's credibility-based refusal of asylum; Moses J had earlier dismissed the application as unarguable apart from a merits attack.
Mr Idubo claimed he had not received notice of the Buxton LJ hearing, but the court found that account untrue and noted substantial delay after the hearing.
The court refused reinstatement because the underlying application had no merit, the delay was unexplained, and the application notice was untruthful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Open-court application to reinstate a judicial review application previously struck out for non-appearance.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the judicial review was not reinstated.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judicial review application has been struck out after being called on in court, the court's discretion under CPR 23.11 to relist it must take account of the merits of the underlying claim as well as delay and the applicant's explanation for non-appearance; an unarguable merits-only challenge will not be revived by repeated reinstatement applications.
legal_issues: Nature of an application to reinstate a struck-out claim
Scope of discretion under CPR 23.11
Whether delay and untruthfulness in the application notice matter
Whether the underlying asylum judicial review was arguable

confidence.notes: Short procedural judgment with clear outcome and reasoning on reinstatement discretion.

notes: TAG Tranche 2 test-case rulings on recoverable ATE premium, referral fees, and indemnity principle.

enrichment.short_title: TAG scheme recoverable ATE premium and referral fees
key_facts: These Accident Group test cases concerned the recoverability of sums charged to claimants under the TAG conditional fee and after-the-event insurance scheme.
Chief Master Hurst held that the full TAG insurance charges of £840 and £997.50 were not wholly recoverable premiums within section 29 of the Access to Justice Act 1999.
Recoverable premium figures were limited to £450 (2000 year), £480 (2001 Lloyds), and £425 (2001 NIG), after deducting collateral elements such as ring-fencing and funding-cost insurance.
The £310 plus VAT AIL payment was a referral fee paid to TAG, breached the Introduction and Referral Code, and was not recoverable as a disbursement.
TAG panel solicitors' obligations to reimburse unrecovered disbursements and cap fees to recovered costs did not breach the indemnity principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further preliminary issues in multi-party Accident Group test cases on TAG scheme costs, following an earlier delegation judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants largely succeeded on the live premium, referral-fee, and indemnity-principle issues; only part of the TAG insurance charge was a recoverable premium and the AIL fee was irrecoverable.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 29 of the Access to Justice Act 1999, not every sum payable by a TAG claimant for insurance is a recoverable premium: collateral or extraneous elements must be stripped out, and referral fees paid through AIL to TAG are not recoverable disbursements where they breach the Introduction and Referral Code.
legal_issues: Meaning of premium under section 29 Access to Justice Act 1999
Recoverability of collateral TAG scheme benefits
Whether AIL and related payments were referral fees
Compliance with the Introduction and Referral Code
Indemnity principle and CFA fee-cap provisions

confidence.notes: Very long judgment, but paragraph-level conclusions on Issues 2, 3, 5, 10-13, 16 and 17 are explicit.

notes: Mesothelioma insurer liable in full despite successive employment periods; rateable proportion clause rejected.

key_facts: Mrs Phillips, as widow and executrix of Arthur Phillips, sued insurers under the Third Parties (Rights against Insurers) Act 1930 for the balance of a £205,000 mesothelioma judgment against Kinkia Limited.
Mr Phillips had been exposed to asbestos during two periods of employment with Kinkia, but the defendants were on risk only between October 1959 and November 1968.
The insurers argued that a standard employer's liability policy condition 6 entitled them to pay only a rateable proportion corresponding to their period on risk.
Eady J held that condition 6 applied only to double insurance at the same time, not successive policies, and that no custom or business-efficacy term justified apportionment between periods of cover.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on construction of historic employer's liability insurance in proceedings under the 1930 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant entitled to judgment; the insurers were not entitled to withhold 27.5% of the judgment debt.
enrichment.ratio: A standard rateable-proportion clause in a mid-twentieth-century employer's liability policy covers concurrent double insurance, not successive periods of cover for an indivisible mesothelioma liability based on continuing negligent exposure; where the insurer was on risk throughout a period of material contribution, it must indemnify the insured in full for that liability.
legal_issues: Construction of condition 6 rateable proportion clauses
Whether successive policies covered the same liability
Application of Fairchild and McGhee causation principles to insurance contracts
Whether a time-exposed apportionment term should be implied
Custom and practice in asbestos long-tail claims

notes: Long-delayed education negligence claim dismissed after trial; no breach or causation proved.

enrichment.short_title: Local authority education negligence claim dismissed
key_facts: Richard Keating claimed that London Borough of Bromley and its employees negligently failed to educate him properly between 1977 and 1986, leaving him with severe educational and employment deficits.
Proceedings began in 1992, survived strike-out in X v Bedfordshire, and proceeded only on vicarious liability for employee negligence after Phelps v Hillingdon.
The claimant had a history of special educational placement, dyslexia-related difficulties, poor motivation, and significant absences from school.

After a fact-heavy trial on very stale evidence, the judge found no negligence by the authority's education officers or employees and no damage to his educational achievements caused by their conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a long-running negligence claim against a local education authority after earlier strike-out and limitation challenges.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant in an education negligence action must prove that local authority employees fell below the standard of care and that this caused identifiable educational damage; after many years' delay, absent or incomplete records and fading witness memory, the claimant failed to establish either breach or causation on the surviving vicarious liability claim.
legal_issues: Vicarious liability of a local education authority
Standard of care owed by teachers and education officers
Causation of educational underachievement
Assessment of special educational needs and placement decisions
Impact of delay and missing records on fact-finding

notes: Composite Court of Appeal judgment resolving multiple Chaudhary race discrimination procedural appeals.

key_facts: Dr Chaudhary, a urologist of Indian ethnic origin, brought multiple employment tribunal claims alleging direct and indirect race discrimination over refusal to award a National Training Number and Specialist Register entry.
His Manchester registrar post had been advertised as Royal College approved but was treated as lacking SAC approval under the post-Calman Orange Guide transition rules.

The Court of Appeal heard together applications for permission to appeal and appeals arising from four sets of tribunal proceedings, including a successful indirect discrimination finding against the BMA.

The court refused permission on Southampton time-limit and Manchester abuse-of-process challenges, granted permission but dismissed the STA jurisdiction appeal, and made a consent order remitting the BMA appeal to the EAT.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Composite Court of Appeal hearing of multiple permission applications and appeals from employment tribunals and the EAT in parallel race discrimination proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed: Southampton time-bar appeal dismissed; Manchester abuse-of-process appeals refused permission; STA jurisdiction appeal dismissed; BMA appeal remitted by consent for full EAT hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Indirect race discrimination claims based on application of a requirement to an individual are not acts extending over a period once the final decision on that application is made; section 54(2) of the Race Relations Act 1976 excludes employment tribunal jurisdiction where a statutory appeal procedure exists against the qualifying body's refusal, and presenting a fresh tribunal claim rather than amending an existing one is not necessarily an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Time limits and acts extending over a period under section 68
Abuse of process and Henderson v Henderson in tribunal litigation
Employment tribunal jurisdiction over STA Specialist Register refusals
Meaning of enactment in section 54(2)
Indirect discrimination against the BMA

notes: Amendment refused on merits and limitation; parasitic loss-of-chance claim time-barred.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor negligence amendment refused as time-barred
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Browning sued their former solicitors, Brachers, for negligence in handling county court litigation over a goat-farming purchase from the Gilhams.
They sought to amend their claim to add a loss-of-chance claim against the original solicitor, Mr Hinchliffe, for inserting a written representations clause in a memorandum of sale.
Master Turner refused permission, holding the proposed claim had no real prospect of success and was statute-barred.

On appeal, Eady J upheld the refusal because the Hinchliffe claim was parasitic on the county court counterclaim and the cause of action accrued when that counterclaim was effectively lost in October 1996.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of review from a master's refusal to permit amendment of a professional negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to amend refused.
enrichment.ratio: A proposed professional negligence claim for loss of a chance to sue an earlier solicitor must have a real prospect of success on its own merits and accrue when the underlying litigation opportunity is lost; where the claim is parasitic on a counterclaim defeated before the later solicitor's retainer ended, limitation is not postponed until the later solicitor's six-year period expires.
legal_issues: Real prospect of success test on amendment applications
Accrual of loss-of-chance claims against successive solicitors
Whether a claim against an earlier solicitor is parasitic on the underlying litigation
Date when limitation begins to run
Review of a master's case-management decision

notes: Spouse exemption under section 102(5) excluded reservation-of-benefit charge on settled property.

enrichment.short_title: Reservation of benefit and spouse exemption
key_facts: Mrs Greenstock settled Beechwood Cottage on trusts giving her husband a life interest and later discretionary benefits for a class including herself.
The property was later sold and replaced with Meadows and an investment bond; she occupied Meadows rent-free until her death.

The Revenue accepted reservation-of-benefit conditions were otherwise satisfied, but the taxpayer argued section 102(5) excluded the charge because the original gift was an exempt transfer to her spouse.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the Revenue's appeal, holding the spouse exemption displaced the reservation-of-benefit provisions for the original gift.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Revenue appeal to the Court of Appeal from Lightman J and the Special Commissioner on inheritance tax reservation-of-benefit provisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; reservation-of-benefit charge excluded by the spouse exemption.
enrichment.ratio: Where property is gifted to a settlement and the transfer is an exempt transfer to the transferor's spouse under section 18 of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984, section 102(5) of the Finance Act 1986 excludes the reservation-of-benefit rules for that gift; the statutory reference to an exempt transfer can be applied directly without subdividing the gift into separate proprietary interests.
legal_issues: Interaction of section 102 Finance Act 1986 with IHTA 1984 exemptions
Whether a gift to settlement must be split into separate interests for section 102 purposes
Effect of spouse exemption on reservation-of-benefit taxation
Application of Ingram v IRC to successive interests

notes: Army libel strike-out and summary judgment refused; claim survives to jury trial.

enrichment.short_title: Army affair libel strike-out application refused
key_facts: Captain Sarah Pedder and Sergeant Allan Dummer sued Associated Newspapers over Evening Standard and Daily Mail articles reporting an alleged affair during Operation Swift Sword in Oman.
The claimants contended the word affair meant an improper sexual relationship during the exercise and that the articles accused them of lying about when the relationship began.
Associated Newspapers applied to strike out the claim or enter summary judgment, relying on admissions, Army Board findings, and alleged abuse of process because of a parallel Sun libel action.
Gray J refused both applications, holding that on the Galbraith test the claimants had a real prospect of establishing meaning, defeating justification, and recovering more than nominal damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant application to strike out or obtain summary judgment in a jury libel trial shortly before the listed trial date.
enrichment.outcome: Applications refused; the libel claim proceeds to trial.
enrichment.ratio: In a jury libel action, strike-out or summary judgment should be granted only if, taking the claimant's case at its highest, no reasonable jury could find for the claimant on meaning, justification, or damages; parallel unfavourable administrative findings do not automatically defeat a defamation claim or make it an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Whether articles bore meanings of sexual misconduct during military exercise and dishonesty
Availability of strike-out and summary judgment in jury libel cases
Application of the Galbraith test
Admissibility and weight of Army Board of Enquiry findings on damages
Abuse of process where related libel proceedings are pending

notes: Hague-Visby one-year time bar runs from final delivery under varied voyage, not rejected Lagos tender.

enrichment.short_title: Hague-Visby time bar and redelivery after rejection

statutes_considered.title: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1971

key_facts: Trafigura charterers claimed against owners of the SONIA for contaminated jet fuel carried from Saudi Arabia to Lagos, where receivers rejected the cargo.
After deviation to Abidjan and agreement to a new voyage, the cargo was delivered at Agioi Theodori in Greece on 1 April 2000.
The owners argued Article III rule 6 of the Hague-Visby Rules barred the claim because suit was not brought within one year of when the cargo should have been delivered at Lagos.
The Court of Appeal held delivery at Agioi Theodori was delivery under the varied charterparty, not an entirely separate transaction, so suit brought on 27 March 2001 was in time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Charterers' appeal from summary judgment for owners on a Hague-Visby Article III rule 6 time-bar application.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; owners not discharged from liability by the one-year time bar.
enrichment.ratio: For Article III rule 6, whether suit is time-barred depends first on whether there was delivery of the goods; where the same cargo remains on board and is later delivered pursuant to a varied or continued contract of carriage after rejection at the original port, that final delivery is relevant delivery and time runs from it rather than from the date delivery should have occurred at the original destination.
legal_issues: Meaning of delivery in Article III rule 6
Whether delivery in Greece was under the same contract of carriage
Distinction between delivery and failure to deliver
Effect of voyage variation after cargo rejection
Whether American 'separate transaction' cases apply
